segments.text: But in the meantime, I think we will already introduce the various panelists that we will have on this panel. We will have on this panel His Excellency Mr. Abdul Kassim Famba, Minister of Youth and Sports, in charge of civic instruction and citizen construction of Mali, whom I ask you to applaud very, very loudly, please. We will also have on this panel the Minister of Youth of Chad, Nair Abakar, whom I ask you to applaud as well.

We will also have Mr. Frédéric Ampia, representative of the PNUD Sierra Leone, on this panel. We will also have Mr. Alassane Diallo, Director General of Youth of Senegal. And this session, the Q&A session will be moderated by Mr. Nana John.

And there will be two testimonies from two young people, one from Mali and one from Sierra Leone, who will share their experiences with us. And at the end, we will have the summary of this session, which will be presented to us by Elisabeth. The summary will be in English.

It will be done by Elisabeth. She comes from Nigeria. And finally, we will have the closing speech of Mr. Minister of Youth and Sports of Mali, who will have the honour of welcoming the YouthConnekt Sahel Session 2027.
And this will be the end of the program with the family photo. If His Excellency is here, we will announce the opening speech. If he is not here, we will invite the panelists to settle in.

As announced, ladies and gentlemen, we will welcome the Minister of Youth of Sierra Leone for his opening speech. Beyond this session, please welcome the Minister of Youth of Sierra Leone for his opening remarks. Thank you very much, Madam Moderator.

Distinguished ministers and government representatives present, development partners, representatives of the African Union, representatives from the United Nations agencies and regional institutions here present, private sector leaders, civil society representatives, and to my fellow young people, good afternoon, bonsoir, tout le monde, comment allez-vous? A round of applause for Mali. I'm so intrigued by your outfit. A nice outfit, Mali.

Are there young people in the room this afternoon? I'm not feeling the vibe. Are there young people in the room this afternoon? Great, great, great. Are there Gen Zs in the house? Then clock it for me, let me feel it.

Good, good, good, good, good. So it is a great honour and privilege for me to be accorded this single opportunity this afternoon to speak on a theme that says bridging regions, empowering youth, and transforming Africa. Viva Africa, viva! But that's too cold, that's too cold.

Africa, we can do it better. Viva Africa, viva! Viva Mali, viva! Viva Sahel, viva! Viva Niger, viva! Viva Rwanda, viva! And viva Sierra Leone, viva! How about Nigeria? Viva Nigeria, viva! How about Senegal? Viva Senegal, viva! Amanza! Great, great, great. Oh! Viva Chad, viva! And a round of applause for Chad.
Thank you, thank you. Burkina Faso, that's one of my favourite African countries. And respect to Ibrahim Charlie.
Viva Burkina Faso, viva! Great, great, great. And viva to all of us, viva. So colleagues, this session reflects the very essence of what YouthConnekt represents.

A powerful platform that connects young people to opportunities, connects ideas to action, and connects nations to a common future. Today we are not merely going to discuss youth development, but to reaffirm a fundamental truth that the future of Africa will be shaped by the aspirations, creativity, resilience, and leadership of its young people. A round of applause for all the young people here present.

Across our two regions, young people constitute the majority of our population. They are entrepreneurs, innovators, peace builders, artists, farmers, scientists, digital creators, and changemakers. They possess the energy to transform economies, the vision to reshape institutions, and the courage to challenge all paradigms and create new pathways for progress.

Despite all of this, we are equally aware that many young people continue to face significant barriers, including unemployment, limited access to finance, skills mismatches, vulnerability to conflict, climate-related challenges, and inadequate participation in the decision-making process. The reality, however, is that these challenges know no borders. Therefore, our response cannot be confined within national boundaries.

It requires strong regional cooperation, commitment to unlocking the immense potential of Africa's youth. Distinguished colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, YouthConnekt has emerged as one of Africa's most successful platforms for youth engagement, empowerment, and transformation. It has demonstrated that when governments and development partners, the private sector, and young people work together, extraordinary outcomes become possible.
YouthConnekt is more than a conference. It is more than a program. It is more than a network.

It is a movement that is empowering a generation of African leaders, innovators, and entrepreneurs to take ownership of Africa's future. Allow me at this juncture to express my profound gratitude and appreciation to Mr. Frederick Ampere, the United Nations Resident Representative in Sierra Leone. A round of applause, please.

Whom I often describe as a true reservoir of knowledge and a steadfast champion of youth empowerment. Thank you, Fred, for your unwavering commitment to believing and advancing the youth empowerment programs in Sierra Leone. Thank you for believing in the wisdom and vision of the Ministry of Youth Affairs and for the confidence you have consistently demonstrated in our ability to deliver transformative programs.

I also wish to extend sincere appreciation to the entire YouthConnekt Secretariat at a time when organizing the first-ever YouthConnekt Manor River Union Regional Forum in Freetown seemed an ambitious and almost impossible undertaking. You believed in the vision. A round of applause for the YouthConnekt Secretariat.

Today, we proudly celebrate the successful inaugural MRU YouthConnekt Forum as a shared achievement and a landmark moment for regional youth cooperation. Colleagues, distinguished guests, the success of the inaugural MRU YouthConnekt Forum was not simply about hosting an event. It was about creating a platform where young people could engage directly with policymakers, development partners, and the private sector.

It was about demonstrating that youth are not passive beneficiaries of development, but architects of solutions, drivers of innovation, and partners in nation-building. As we reflect on the experiences emerging from both the Sahel and MRU regions, one lesson becomes abundantly clear. Meaningful youth empowerment requires institutionalization.

We must move beyond one-off engagements and establish sustainable mechanisms that guarantee continuous youth participation. We must strengthen governance, structures for regional youth forums, mobilize long-term resources, and create permanent channels for dialogue between young people and decision-makers. Our ambition must be to transform regional youth forums into enduring institutions capable of driving policy innovation, fostering entrepreneurship, promoting regional cohesion, and sustaining youth-led development efforts for generations to come.

Ladies and gentlemen, the future prosperity of our regions depends on the strength of our partnership, not just our natural resources. I therefore call for strengthening bilateral and multilateral collaboration among member states of the Mano River Union and the Sahel. Let us deepen cooperation in youth entrepreneurship and enterprise development, technical and vocational skills development, digital innovation, and emerging technologies, cross-border trade and investment opportunities, climate adaptation and green economic initiatives, and above all, peace-building and social cohesion.

By working together, we can unlock economies of scale, leverage our collective strengths, and create ecosystems where young people can innovate, compete, thrive beyond national borders. Our vision should be a region where a young entrepreneur in free time can collaborate seamlessly with counterparts in Bamako, in Burkina Faso, in Conakry, in Dakar, in Chad, in Nami, and even Morovia or Nigeria, where innovation transcends borders, where opportunities are shared, and where regional integration creates prosperity for all. To our development partners and private sector stakeholders present, I urge you to continue investing in youth-led solutions.

Investing in youth is not merely a social responsibility. It is the smartest economic investment any nation can make. And above all, to us now, to my colleague young people, to my fellow young people, to my fellow Africans, especially those gathered here today, I leave you with a challenge and a charge.

But before this charge, I just want to remind you that Africa as a whole constitutes about 30.7 million kilometers of land, which is about 11.7 million miles. And above all, despite this barrage acreage of land, Africa still imports about $100 billion on food annually. Africa also constitutes about 30% of the world's precious or critical minerals.

And above all, despite all these natural resources, we still grapple with underemployment and unemployment. So, our fellow young people, let me ask you this question. If we are to leave to see Agenda 2063, what Africa do you envision? If we are to leave and to see Agenda 2063, how do you see yourself contributing to that vision, which you are envisioning for Africa? Do not allow yourselves to be defined by the challenges before you.

Be defined by the solutions you create. Be the generation that transforms adversity into opportunity, division into unity, and ideas into industries. Africa needs young entrepreneurs who will create jobs rather than seek them.

Africa needs young leaders who will champion peace over conflict, cooperation over competition, and action over excuses. Today, I call upon every young person here present, every African, whether you are here or out there, become a builder of nations, a driver of innovation, and a champion of regional integration. Let us build businesses that cross borders.

Let us create innovations that solve African problems. Let us forge partnerships that unite our people. Let us transform our talents into prosperity, our ideas into enterprises, and our ambitions into lasting impact.
Remember this, no man is an island, and no man stands alone. Nobody is coming to build Africa for us, Africa for Africans. Africa's future will not be built by resources alone.

Africa's future will not be built by one nation alone. It will be built by the imagination of young people, the courage of its innovators, and the determination of a generation that refuses to inherit problems without creating solutions. My young brothers and sisters, the story of Africa's transformation is not a story that will be written for you.

It is a story that will be written by you and by all of us. Let us stop complaining, and let us stop foreseeing the challenges ahead of us. Let us be the solution that we imagine, and let us create the necessary infrastructure that will propel and enhance that solution.

If our generation has the courage to think boldly, innovate relentlessly, and work together across borders, there is no challenge too great, no obstacle too difficult, and no dream too ambitious for Africa to achieve. So I conclude, colleagues. Let me say this.

As we continue the important conversations during this summit, let us lead this session with renewed determination to strengthen cooperation between our regions, expand opportunities for our youth, and build systems that empower future generations. No African country can do this alone. Africa is the reservoir of wealth, not just in natural resource reserves, but even in our talents.
Let our cultural diversity strengthen and embody us. Let it don't weaken us. And therefore, colleagues, I want you to be bold with me this afternoon to say, together we can.
Say with me, together we can. Together we can. We can build a more prosperous Africa.
Together we can. Together we can. We can build a more peaceful Africa.
Together we can. Together we can. We can build a more innovative Africa.
Together we can. Together we can. And together we can ensure that African century is powered by the talent, creativity, and leadership of Africa's young people.
I believe in it, and I want you to believe in it. And I want to thank you all. God bless you.
God bless Africa. Together we can. A round of applause, please, for His Excellency, the Ministry of Youth, because Africa for Africa, youth for Africa, and together, yes, we can do great things.
Thank you very much for your speech. Allow me now to introduce our intervenants for this session. We will now call on Mr. Minister of Youth of Mali to join us.
I would like to welcome them, please. Mr. Minister of Youth of Chad. Mr. Representative of Sierra Leone.
Mr. Alassane Diallo, Director General of Youth of Senegal. The Minister of Youth of Sierra Leone. The Ministry of Youth of Sierra Leone.

Thank you. So, ladies and gentlemen, I will now introduce Mr. Minister of Youth of Mali, in charge of civic instruction and citizen construction, for his speech. I would like to welcome him with an ovation, please.

Good evening, everyone. Honorable Ministers, Honorable Ministers here from Sierra Leone, my brother from Chad, also the Director of Senegal, and also the PNUD, that's right, the PNUD. Thank you to the PNUD partners.

Thank you to all of you for coming to this plenary. I think that today's speeches will focus on what we are doing as a forum in our different countries. I think that the most experienced today on stage is perhaps my brother from Chad, who has already held the YouthConnekt Sahel at their level.

Today, at the level of Mali, we have a few ambitions. Very strong ambitions. Because one of the strong statements of the President of the Transition, the General of the Army, Assimi Goïda, President of the Transition, Head of State of Mali, he said that if he failed, it would be all of Mali's youth that would fail.

What does that mean? It means that today, as part of his mission, he has put youth at the heart of all sectors that are moving in Mali. To do this, he gave us firm instructions. How can we work with youth today? How can we no longer speak in the place of youth and put youth at the center of concerns, put youth at the forefront of their concerns, to meet the expectations that this youth has expressed? We wanted to organize the General States of Youth first.

The General States of Youth, let's say 40 years later, was the first major meeting of youth at the level of Mali. These General States have allowed all stakeholders, at the municipal, regional, national level, as well as in 37 diaspora countries, including some who came from Rwanda, to come to Mali to discuss the aspirations of youth, in all sectors. As a result of this, 256 recommendations were made.

Among these 256 recommendations, a classification was made on the short-term, medium-term and long-term. As a result of this, the President set up a commission at the level of the Presidency called the SINSER-FNR. It is a commission that evaluates the various recommendations of the General States of Youth.

At this stage, every year, the SINSER-FNR evaluates these documents and then tries to see how, today, at the level of the Department and in the other sectors of the State, the other sectors are taking into account the aspirations of this youth. Today, this is where we are in relation to youth. But you know, in our sector, we have youth, in Mali, we have sport and civic instruction.

We also had to find an articulation between what youth is doing, sport, which is also a framework that brings youth together, and civic instruction. So, the President decided to give instructions to renovate all the regional stadiums at the level of Bamako, which served to hold the first Cannes 2002, which had been organized in Mali. These renovations have been made and they are still underway.

At this stage, today, we have 11 sports infrastructures that have been renovated at the level of Mali, and a few youth infrastructures, notably the Palais des Pionniers and some youth houses that have been renovated following the support of the PLUD. For the stadiums and educational infrastructures, these stadiums and educational infrastructures have been 100% renovated with the State budget. Now, what had to be done? How can sport today contribute to creating employment? That was a big question.

So, we had to find a way to make sport profitable enough, to make these infrastructures profitable enough so that young people can, beyond other sectors, also benefit from the opportunities that exist in the sports sector. Today, we have stadiums that are starting to bring in money because sport, we have reminded the sports community that sport is a business. Sport brings in money.

It's not just in Africa that we're behind. There was an assessment that was made in what sport brings in the world, especially in Africa, and we're talking about billions of dollars that are brought in by sport. Africa doesn't even have 0.1%. That means that we have a lot of effort to make on this.

How can we, more and more, get involved so that this sport is profitable enough for our young people? Because young people's aspirations are very high. I have a lot to say. I don't know how much time I have, but otherwise, in this context, we have given instructions to those who manage our infrastructures.

The management of infrastructures at this level is to see all that is at the level of stadium management, especially stadium directors, to put themselves at the disposal of commercial agents. How can they mobilize money around our sporting infrastructures? And how, through the events that take place at the stadium level, can we recruit as many young people as possible? As an example, the last game there was in Bamako, between Mali and Rwanda, in Bamako, and... I won't tell you the score, but what is important is what the game brought. We were able to mobilize, just for this game, 115 million francs CFA.

And we recruited 1,000 young people just for the management of these stadiums. This means that there are possibilities, but we have to think much further. The advantage of our youth today is that it is anchored in new technologies.
We have artificial intelligence. And this new technology, for example, in the mobilization of this fund, we sold tickets 100% online. There were zero physical tickets.

All the tickets that were sold were online. This means that today, if we strengthen this position, you are the actors of the new technology. You are the ones who have the knowledge of artificial intelligence.

You have at your disposal, at least for young Malians, and I'm sure it's the same dynamic today in our different countries, you have the new technology. You have to put yourself in a position to say how we can more involve this new technology in the management of our infrastructures, in the management of our ministry, of our various ministries, especially the Ministry of Youth and Sports. So today, it's in this dynamic that we are.

And we are also in a process to see at the level of youth how the sport business, that is, if you have action plans at the level of sport, how we can finance this sport business through the mobilization of the funds that are made at the level of sport. And I think it's this same dynamic that is underway at the level of certain elements of the youth structure. In addition, we have the National Council of Youth.

You know, for a long time, the National Council of Youth had been pointed out as being more of a group of young people who opposed the decisions of the state or who went against the decisions of the state. At the level of Mali, we discussed with the young people following the General States of Youth to see what model of the National Council of Youth they themselves wanted. So we finally restructured the National Council of Youth with new texts, new approaches, and we kept the strict respect of the 35 years.

That is, beyond 35 years, you can no longer and you should no longer be in the National Council of Youth. So that's a major evolution that we've had. And today, I can tell you very honestly, as the Minister in charge of youth, we are extremely proud of our National Council of Youth for the efforts that are being made.
Thank you very much, Mr. Minister. With the microphone, we can continue. But I will just finish on this point with the National Council of Youth.

It is still extremely important. The restructuring of the National Council of Youth has led us to introduce young people in all the administrative councils, let's say essential, that we have at the level of the country, but also in certain directions. Today we find them in the National Council of Transition, which plays the office of parliament at the level of Mali, the High Council of Collectivities and in several institutions of this kind.

And in this context, given the efforts they are making, because we saw the young people at the level of Mali when we had experienced some crises, the young people came out naturally to help in the fuel crisis. Very recently, there were some young people who left Guinea for problems they had and we through the young people and the security forces accompanied these young people so that they could join their country. And the young people did it for free and really they were there morning, noon, evening.

The President of the Transition has finally decided to give a budget line to the National Council of Youth. So every year, the National Council of Youth has a budget line of about 100 million that is designed for their own movements. These are not their activities, but for their movements, certain initiatives at the local level.
This allows them to be able to affirm their position more. And the Council has been opened. It is no longer a question of being a member of the National Council of Youth.

Any association of youth must be able to benefit from the support of the formations of the National Council of Youth. So at this stage, this is what I could say about youth and I will stay open for questions. Thank you.
Thank you very much, Mr. Le Ministre. You had a bonus. We will frame it with the timing because it is five minutes per speaker.

Five minutes per speaker, of course, because we will also have sessions of testimony and also questions and answers. So now, I will give the floor to Mr. Le Ministre de la Jeunesse of Chad, Mr. Nair Abakar. You can do your intervention on the spot.

He will tell us about the experience as a country having organized the YouthConnekt Sahel in 2025 and, of course, the key factors of success to transform the energy of this gathering into a sustainable and concrete action for young people. Mr. Le Ministre, you have five minutes. Five minutes.

Well, I am a little jealous of my colleague from Mali, but we will try to do it with the five minutes. Anyway, first of all, thank you very much for the speech. I would like to greet my brother, the Minister of Mali, especially the Minister of Sierra Leone, the Director General of the Youth of Senegal and the representative of UNHCR who is sharing with us this afternoon this panel.

Before talking about the YouthConnekt experience in Chad, I would also like to talk about what Chad has done for the youth of Chad and also for the youth of Africa for more than 10 years. Let's go back in time. In 2016, peace to his soul, Marshal Idris Deby was appointed by his father at the 54th summit of the African Union as champion of the theme of the year.

And the theme of the year was to take full advantage of the demographic dividend by investing in youth. And he raised this issue very high and gave the very first Pan-African youth forum which took place in Jamena if I'm not mistaken on the 29th of the 1st of July. And this Pan-African forum was one of the very first held by the African Union and by its partners which was able to bring together all the African youth as a whole to listen to their grievances but also to write a document of recommendation which will be, three days later, presented by the President in front of the 54 other African countries.

And this document gave the very first Pan-African youth fund which is now housed at the level of the African Union. And all the African countries contribute to this fund and this fund is accessible to all young project leaders. And this, when I speak to you about this, is already in 2016.

So, exactly 10 years ago. Today, under the impetus of Maréchal Mbamatidris Debidno, Chad continues its efforts to enrich the youth of its country but also the youth of Africa. This is why, last year, the Chad government wanted to organize YouthConnekt Sahel which saw the participation of the Sahel countries but also of the neighbouring countries who sent their young people and this also allowed us to bring together the entire Chadian youth in Jamena to speak and above all discuss the prosperity of the youth in general.

It was a great experience for our country because today YouthConnekt is institutionalized in Chad. It is under the tutelage of the Ministry of Youth and Sports and this program is judged and has the same value as a state institution. In other words, it has a budget, it has a coordinator, it has employees.

Just to show you how important youth is in Chad. And following this program, this forum, we were also able to organize contests to highlight the national talents but above all the talents of the Sahel where there are Chadians who won the prize, also our Nigerian brothers and Burkina Faso if I'm not mistaken who had won prizes where they were distinguished. And so for us, it is an experience that must be repeated.

Repeated because it highlights the young people, it highlights their talents and we have noticed unfortunately that in Africa we have very few platforms that highlight youth. And so, if I take the words of my colleague, today, bringing young people together is something very complicated. Not only at the national level but at the international level.

That's why I hope that for the next YouthConnekt and above all the next regional forums we will be able to take advantage of this moment together to come up with recommendations and above all to put in place strong actions that don't need to wait a year to be implemented. Because today, we may be able to bring youth together, we may be able to highlight them but the question that we have at the end of the day is the question of funding that no one wants to address. But this is the reality, unfortunately.

All the young people in this room and elsewhere have very beautiful projects for their country. They want to help with development but today, our tool is not complete. It is a tool for pleading but we don't have a continuation and we don't have a solution for these young people.

And so I hope, at the end of this panel and even beyond this panel maybe for the closing that we, ministers and all the other authorities that are here, will be able to put in place a real policy of youth support that is sustainable. So this is my message. I hope I have respected the five minutes.

Of course you have respected the time. Thank you very much, Mr. Minister of Youth of Chad. We will now give the floor to Mr. Frédéric Ampia representative of Sierra Leone who will speak to us beyond this year's inaugural forum what institutional frameworks or mechanisms are needed to ensure that regional youth networks are inclusive, adequately resourced and capable of delivering real impacts.

Thank you very much Madam Moderator. Ministers here from Mali, Sierra Leone my brother and all senior Chad and my senior colleagues who are here. This is a very difficult question you're asking me but I will try to deal with it the best way I can.

I'm speaking a little bit slowly because when I speak fast they have problems. So I will speak slowly. So now my minister talked about my passion for youth and my commitment to youth issues and that is where I will start my submission from.

I am from Ghana. And I am sure that everybody in this room knows of Dr. Kwame Nkrumah and Kwame Nkrumah had one rallying call which is Africa must unite. If I take Guinea President Seketure was about 36 years when he became president.
At 23 he was a secretary of the postal union. If I take formerly he was about 40 when he became president. But the struggle started way beyond.

Kwame Nkrumah himself was 36 years when he started the movement. So in those days they did not have internet but they were able to connect because they knew the power of connectivity. The power of young people coming together to share ideas and that generation had the responsibility of taking us out of colonial rule.

Our generation have the responsibility of getting us that economic independence that we seek. And that can only happen if the youth lead the way. And if the youth are given the platform and opportunity to lead, equip them, support them but more importantly assist them to vision and bring their vision to reality.

So that's my starting point. Now we talk about MRU, YouthConnekt and all of that. I'll start by saying that I've had the unique opportunity of working as one of the key people to do the first Sahel YouthConnekt in Senegal.

I was based in Senegal in the West African hub West Central Africa and we organized the first Sahel YouthConnekt. Now what was the inspiration behind that? UNDP at the time, we believed that we need to change the narrative of Africa. A narrative of conflict.
A narrative of poverty into an opportunity. That this is a new Africa. This is the Sahel that we know it is not the Sahel of poverty, of drought, of conflict.

We needed to change the narrative. And so we had what we call the Sahel Offer. An offer that mobilized more than 100 million dollars through our regional stabilization program to be able to address key issues that confronted us in the Sahel.

But then we needed to create the opportunity for young people to come together because it's not enough to create the platform. We needed to bring young people together to ideate, to share ideas, and more importantly, to share their own aspirations on how they build networks and move ahead. I was fortunate enough, again, that my former staff was the YouthConnekt director, Ule Keita.
She is from Mali. The immediate past director of YouthConnekt. So we reached out to her and said there's nothing like a regional YouthConnekt.
And we think that the youth of Sahel need a space, need a platform, need a voice. And so we want to do a YouthConnekt Sahel. She said, well, why not? And that was, the rest was history.
We organized it and now I'm happy to know that it has moved on to other countries and the like. Fast forward, I find myself in Sierra Leone. And the same questions confront us.

My first experience was trying to mobilize resources from a big multinational donor to do some work in Sierra Leone and a private sector entity. And they told me, the first question they asked me was how much, how many people are in Sierra Leone? What's the population? I said maybe around 8 million. They said, well, 8 million, that's a small market.
I said, wait a minute. When we talk about Sierra Leone and the market of Sierra Leone, we are not talking about only Sierra Leone. We are talking about the Mano River Union Market.

They said to me, now you are talking. Which meant that the force of our collective union, the force of our collective resources and our youth was something that placed us in a very competitive world in the world market. And that was where the inspiration came from.

Now, so the first thing was, how do we get our youth in the Sahel to change that narrative of conflict of civil wars and all of that? Because still today, when you Google Sierra Leone, Liberia, most of the times you see civil wars and things like that. We've gone past that. We're at a point where we want to change the narrative of opportunity, the narrative of investment.
And for that to happen, it's for the youth to lead the way. And it's for us to support them and provide a platform for them. And that is why we started talking about the MRE YouthConnekt.

And thanks to the government and the minister and his team, we were able to mobilize the resources. The institutional framework you're talking about, it came about because we needed private sector investment in it. We had to create a platform.

We had to create the logic and the raison d'etre for others to invest in it. And that's the role of UNDP, to provide our catalytic funding, to mobilize user convenient power in our networks, to bring people around the table. And that's exactly what we did.

And then I give you a story to conclude on why the platform was important. In 2023 or thereabouts, or 2021-22, when we did the first Sahel YouthConnekt, we brought 50 youth from across the region. And we did a boot camp and a campaign and a competition.
The person who won the competition came from Nigeria. And his idea was on what you call animation. He had a company that was doing animation for Netflix.

But his challenge was he needed a lot of young people who can code, who can do animation, and he didn't have enough of them in Nigeria. So at the end of the day, we selected from every country young people and sent them to Nigeria for six weeks in Lagos, on boot camp. And guess what? The person that we sent from Sierra Leone, I was still based in Dakar, but Sierra Leone country office sent somebody.

We sent a person to Lagos. Fast forward, I arrive, 2023, in Sierra Leone. And at some point, I asked my colleagues, where is the young man that we sent from the YouthConnekt to Lagos? They told me he's in Makeni.
His name is Amazada Lulu. You see, now he knows him. So we sent this guy to Lagos on boot camp for six weeks to learn animation.

And today, I'm happy to say he's the most sophisticated graphic design animation consultant in Makeni. He's already been in free time. Applause And what is even more exciting is that when I visited him unannounced, I just went to Makeni and I got his contact.

I called him and I said, young man, you are Lulu? He said yes. I said, where are you? Where is your office? And he said he directed us to the office. By the way, when I came to free time, I asked for him.
He came, he needed some support. So we gave him some money, support to buy computers and some other cameras and others. And this is the kind of investment that we talk about.
$15,000 only we invested in him. I visited him unannounced. When I got there, in his studio, he had 20 young women training there on animation.

He was doing jobs for Dutch Vela, for Netflix, and charging $6,000, $10,000 sitting in Makeni. Applause This is the power of YouthConnekt. And so as we embark on this, the lessons that we learn and the frameworks that I like to talk about is, how do you build on these experiences? How do we use our young people as the road or the architecture within which we build regional integration? Because they connect.
Now we have the connecting capabilities. We have the internet, we have everything and we have this platform. How do we harness this platform? By shaping them in the right direction.

How do we maximize so they can trade? And how do we take the barriers to trade, the barriers to investment so that they can trade from Burkina Faso to Niger, Mali to Cote d'Ivoire to Ghana and beyond. Thank you very much. Applause Thank you very much for sharing this experience with us.

So, now we are going to give the floor to Mr. Alassane Diallo. He is the Director General of the Senegal Youth and he is going to talk to us about innovative solutions from the YouthConnekt Sahel that could be, of course, extended to other regions. Mr. Director General, the floor is yours.

Thank you very much, Madam Moderator. First of all, I would like to present the apologies of Madam Minister of Youth and Sports of Senegal who has a conflict of last-minute agenda because she has scheduled field visits for the different stadiums in Rwanda.
